tagline.text: Coffins on limestone cliffs and the burial tradition of the Applai people

location.label: Location
location.text: Echo Valley below St. Mary's Church, Sagada town, Mountain Province

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–700 (per person, covering registration, guide and local transport; Manila round trip not included)

children.text: The hanging coffins of Sagada are an old burial custom of the Applai people, who place wooden coffins on limestone cliffs. You can see them in Echo Valley, reached on foot from St. Mary's Church in town through the cemetery, and the rule is to view them respectfully with a guide.

Sagada is a highland town in Mountain Province, set at about 1,472 m in the Cordillera mountains. According to Wikipedia it is about 18 km from the provincial capital Bontoc and about 388 km from Manila. What makes the town most famous among visitors to the Philippines are its "hanging coffins" on limestone cliffs. Pine coffins are hung from cliffs with ropes and wires or placed at cave mouths. Local accounts say the custom goes back about 2,000 years, but there are almost no written records and the knowledge was passed down orally, so the exact origin is unknown.

The coffins are easiest to see at Echo Valley, a place the villagers regard as sacred. A path beside St. Mary's Episcopal Church leads past the town cemetery into a wooded trail, and across the valley you can see coffins lined up on the cliff face. The older coffins have faded and some have collapsed. The name makes it easy to assume this is a place to shout and hear an echo, but locals ask visitors not to shout, except when a fresh burial is being announced to the community. This is still a community's burial ground before it is a tourist attraction.

There are rules about who is placed in a coffin and how. Wikipedia and several guides say that a person who has married and has grandchildren is eligible, and some accounts add that those who died natural deaths qualify. Following the belief that the body should leave the earth in the same way it entered it, the body was placed in a curled, fetal position, and under Christian influence longer coffins were later used as well. According to one local blog the funeral lasts five days and requires the sacrifice of at least 21 pigs, dogs or chickens. The body is also said to be smoked and propped on a chair. Details vary between sources, so listen to your local guide's explanation as well.

Most people in Sagada today are Episcopalian or Catholic, and the custom of hanging coffins has become much rarer. One blog says the most recent coffin hung at Echo Valley was in June 2008, but this could not be verified, so treat it as a reference only. St. Mary's Church was built by American Episcopal missionaries led by Rev. John Staunton, who also founded St. Mary's School in 1904. Traditional burial customs and Christian faith exist side by side in the same town, which is part of what makes Sagada distinctive. While you stay, ask carefully about funerals and faith, and do not cross the lines your guide sets.

blocks.title: The hanging coffins of Echo Valley

children.text: This is the place in Sagada where you can see the most coffins in one spot. Older coffins and relatively recent ones are mixed along the cliffs, and the basic way to see them is from the viewpoint, following where your guide points.

blocks.title: St. Mary's Church and the cemetery path

children.text: On the way to Echo Valley you pass the Episcopal church and the town cemetery. The cemetery also has graves and plaques of war veterans, so you get a glimpse of Sagada's modern history too.

Coffins are stacked at the entrance of Lumiang Cave. One guide says the cave's environment has preserved coffins about 500 years old, and that the Applai believe the dead need light to find their way home, so coffins are placed only where light reaches.

blocks.title: The meaning of the fetal position

children.text: Placing the body in a curled position is said to mean leaving this earth in the same form as at birth. Hearing your guide explain this helps you see it not as a sight to tick off but as a ritual about life and death.
The gorge is especially striking on a foggy morning. The forest trail down through the pines is enjoyable to walk in its own right.

On All Saints' Day, November 1, villagers light bonfires of old pinewood at the graves in a custom called panag-apoy. Lighting is said to take place around 5–6 PM, and Wikivoyage asks visitors not to photograph the ceremony or go near the graves.
According to the town tourism office, rock climbing at Echo Valley costs ₱200 per person including gear and guide. Keep it separate from the hanging-coffin area.

children.text: Register at the tourism information office in town and keep the receipt. If you need a guide, this is the easiest place to find one.

Look quietly at the coffins on the cliff from the viewpoint. Do not touch them or shout.
Climb back up and rest at a cafe in town or have lunch at the market.
This route ends on foot within the town, so it combines easily with other plans in the afternoon.

Bontoc is about 18 km from Sagada, and travel time depends on the weather.
You can land at Clark International Airport (CRK), travel to Baguio and then take a bus to Sagada.
There is no airport in Sagada, so overland travel is the basis of every itinerary.

According to Wikipedia, Sagada has a subtropical highland climate with average daytime highs of about 19°C in December and about 28°C in July. Annual rainfall averages about 2,835 mm, most of it from May to October, with August the wettest month and January the driest.
Wikivoyage describes the hiking season as the November–May dry season. In the wet season the paths are slippery and some sections may be restricted, so put safety first.

Around All Saints' Day (November 1), many people come to see the panag-apoy bonfire ceremony and the town gets crowded. However, Wikivoyage asks visitors not to photograph the ceremony or approach the graves, so if you visit then, book your lodging early and watch quietly.

There are many guesthouses and homestays around the town center (Poblacion). Lodging prices listed on Wikivoyage were about ₱200–350 per person per night, and some entries date from 2016, so many places now cost more; confirm when you book. Rooms fill quickly during holidays and around All Saints' Day.

Restaurants listed in guides include Yoghurt House, Bilig Cafe, Salt & Pepper, St. Joe's Cafe and Bana's Coffee. Nights in town get dark early, there is a curfew and few places stay open late, so it is best to eat dinner early.

The town has a market and small eateries close together, so you can get around on foot. Since many activities are done with a guide, lodging close to the tourism office and St. Mary's Church is convenient. If you plan to watch the sunrise, ask your host the day before how to get there.
Register first at the tourism information office in town and keep the receipt. It is needed for access to tourist sites.
Guides are still said to be required at Echo Valley as of 2025. It is easy to get lost.
Do not touch or move the coffins or bones. Locals consider it very bad luck.
Bring non-slip sneakers and a light rain jacket.
Mornings are cold, so a thin jacket is useful.
Photos are allowed, but refrain from taking them if a funeral is under way or family members are present.
The All Saints' bonfire ceremony is not a spectacle, so follow the request not to photograph it or go near the graves.
Greet locals you meet along the Echo Valley path politely, and ask permission before taking their photo.
Asking your guide about burial customs and how the town has changed makes the time at the coffins much richer. Tipping is optional, but confirm the set guide fee first.
This is a sacred burial ground of the Applai people before it is a tourist attraction. Shouting, touching the coffins and intrusive photography are a serious insult to locals.
After rain, the dirt paths and rocks are very slippery and the risk of injury is high.
In the wet season, access to some sections may be restricted or guides may refuse to go.
Guide and registration fees differ between sources, so confirm the exact amounts at the local information office.
Facilities are limited and moving around at night is difficult. Pay attention to curfew times and lighting.
Reports mention local complaints about rapid tourism growth and travel agencies commercializing traditions. Follow the rules.
